title: AFFECTIVE EVALUATIONS OF AND REACTIONS TO EXTERIOR AND INTERIOR VEHICLE AUDITORY QUALITY
research_question: How do individuals react to and affectively evaluate sounds, how is preference related to affective reactions induced by sounds, and what is the correlation between affective reactions to sound and sound quality metrics?

participants.description: Undergraduates (N=20, mean age 25.2 yrs, SD 6.1; N=48, mean age 22.8 yrs, SD 4.7; N=42, mean age 26.2 yrs, SD 4.5) from Chalmers University of Technology, Göteborg, with normal hearing.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 20 binaural recordings of interior aircraft sounds (16 original from turboprop/jet, 4 synthesized to vary loudness, tonality, sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength). Range: dBA 52–81, Roughness 0.4-0.8 asper, Fluctuation strength 0.19-0.72 vacil, Tonality 0.10-0.23 Ws, Sharpness 0.77–1.30 acum.

12 binaural recordings of exterior car sounds from six small/medium four-cylinder diesel/gasoline cars. Recorded under wide open throttle acceleration (1000-3000 r.p.m. with 100 r.p.m./s constant acceleration) and throttle pulses. Range: dBA 60–101, Roughness 0.10–0.94 asper, Fluctuation strength 0.06-0.90 vacil, Tonality 0.07-0.69 Ws, Sharpness 0.61-1.12 acum.

mechanisms: Affective reactions and evaluations are overlapping constructs, but conceptually distinct (reactions refer to self, evaluations to sound quality).
Preference for affective reactions is mediated by valence and activation (pleasure-arousal hypothesis).
Liking increases with decreasing loudness and tonality.
Affective reactions are related to core affect (Russell & Feldman-Barret).
moderators: Activation (moderates the relationship between valence and preference, as per pleasure-arousal hypothesis)
Type of sound (stationary interior aircraft vs. time-varying exterior vehicle, influencing range of activation ratings)
implementation_implications: Affect is an important component in product auditory quality optimization, aiming to minimize negative responses and maximize positive responses.
Assessing subjective reactions in terms of valence, activation, and preference is beneficial over only preference.
Future research should investigate physical determinants of valence and activation and develop sound quality metrics that account for time variation.

tables.description: Regression coefficients for the combined regression analyses of preference, affective reactions and psychoacoustic correlates in Experiment 3 (standardized beta weights and explained variance are shown). The upper graph shows the full model, where preference is mediated by valence and activation. The lower graph shows the reduced model, where preference is directly related to psychoacoustic correlates.

limitations: Restricted variation in the activation dimension in Experiments 1 and 2 may have prevented fitting the quadratic and interaction terms of the pleasure-arousal hypothesis.
Existing sound quality metrics are not well suited for time-varying signals, providing only a rough estimate summed over time.
Affective ratings are an average of the affect experienced over the whole time course of the auditory stimuli.
Future research should investigate physical determinants of valence and activation.
Future research should develop sound quality metrics that take into account time variation.
Future research should investigate affective reactions to other auditory stimuli, including sound environments with multiple sound sources.
Future research should use other assessment methods such as continuous ratings and psychophysiological measures.
